meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If it is not right, do not do it. If it is not true, do not say it'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 12.17). The exact wording is George Long's public-domain 1862 translation; later versions differ.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely from Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations, Book 12, §17. The exact English wording you see — “If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it” — is the public-domain 1862 translation by classical scholar George Long ↗. The popular one-liner reproduces Long almost verbatim, changing only his colon to a full stop; later translators word the same passage differently.

source.excerpt: If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it.
trail: Found genuine in Meditations Book 12, §17, in the George Long translation ↗, which reads “If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it.”
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line among Marcus Aurelius’s genuine quotations (Book XII, 17), not under ‘Misattributed’ or ‘Disputed.’
The wording is translation-specific: the 1944 Farquharson edition ↗ renders the same passage “If it is not right, don’t do it: if it is not true, don’t say it.”
source.excerptNote: The opening of Meditations 12.17 in George Long’s 1862 translation; the passage continues with an exhortation to keep one’s judgements one’s own.
source.rightsNote: The Greek original is ancient and long out of copyright, and the exact English wording shown is George Long’s translation, first published in 1862 (London: Bell and Daldy) — well before 1931 and firmly in the public domain in the United States. Note that other renderings of this same passage may still be under copyright: A. S. L. Farquharson’s 1944 Oxford translation (“don’t do it… don’t say it”), for example, is not public domain.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: About Marcus Aurelius
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius (121–180 AD) was Roman emperor from 161 until his death and the last of the so-called ‘Five Good Emperors.’ While campaigning on the northern frontier he kept a private notebook of Stoic self-exhortations in Greek, never intended for publication, now known as the Meditations. Its twelfth and final book gathers some of his tersest rules for conduct — among them the maxim on doing right and speaking truth.

misattribution.heading: The catch
misattribution.intro: This one is authentic — but the viral version quietly hides which translation it is, and tidies up the punctuation.

items.why: The exact phrasing that circulates is George Long’s public-domain rendering of Meditations 12.17, almost always posted with no translator credit. Internet Classics Archive ↗

Long joined the two clauses with a colon (“…do not do it: if it is not true…”) and set them at the head of a longer meditation; the meme swaps in a full stop and lifts the maxim out of its passage. Different translators also word it differently — Farquharson’s 1944 Oxford version uses ‘don’t.’ Wikisource ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and these words are really Marcus Aurelius’s — Meditations Book 12, §17, here in George Long’s 1862 translation. Internet Classics Archive ↗

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Marcus Aurelius never wrote the Meditations for readers. They are a private notebook of Stoic reminders, composed in Greek during the 170s AD while he governed and campaigned, and addressed only to himself. Book 12, the last, is the most compressed — short rules he could recall in a moment of pressure.

Section 17 is one of those rules: a two-part test for action and speech. Do nothing you judge wrong; say nothing you judge false. Stripped to a single line, it reads as a modern integrity slogan — which is exactly why it thrives online, usually without the surrounding thought about keeping one’s own judgement in one’s own power.
